entries.title: 📖 Samuelson's Economics
entries.content:
Paul Samuelson's Economics (1948) is the most influential introductory textbook ever - nineteen editions, four million copies sold, forty-one languages. It popularized the neoclassical synthesis, fusing neoclassical economics with Keynesian economics into the dominant paradigm of mainstream economics for the second half of the 20th century. William Nordhaus joined as co-author for the 17th edition (2001) and contributed the environmental economics sections. The book also coined the paradox of thrift. Attacked by conservatives during the Second Red Scare as communist sympathizers - accusations that continued into the 1980s - it succeeded where Lorie Tarshis's competing Keynesian textbook was marginalized, largely due to Samuelson's dispassionate, scientific style.

entries.title: 🪶 New York Times - Land Acknowledgments Aren't Just Woke. They're Right.
entries.content:
The New York Times recently ran an opinion piece making the case for land acknowledgments as a necessary recognition of historical reality rather than mere virtue signaling. The argument centers on confronting the uncomfortable truth of colonial dispossession rather than glossing over it.

Doc Riter pushes back hard on that framing, asking pointed questions: if our ancestors benefited from systems of oppression, does awareness automatically produce guilt? Is guilt the point? And more practically, how does acknowledgment translate into material repair: reparation, just compensation, or expropriation?

Those are fair questions. Acknowledgment can be performative if it ends at words. But refusing to acknowledge the history also does nothing to address the material consequences that persist to this day. The tension between recognition and action remains unresolved, and that tension is exactly where the conversation ought to stay.

entries.title: 🤖 New York Times - Unleash the Technocrats!
entries.content:
Another New York Times piece champions the "technocrat" solution: let credentialed experts cut through politics and deliver abundance, especially on housing and regulation. Doc Riter isn't buying the brand.

The skepticism starts with the proposed fixes. Pointing to Europe's lower pilot hour requirements or demanding the federal government override local zoning to punish recalcitrant jurisdictions feels less like sound policy than abstract engineering. "No thanks" to trading local control for a top-down diktat.

The inflation diagnosis also misses the blame game. The cost of living spike came under Biden, not Trump's tariffs, but both approaches aim at the same stated goal: lower prices. One tries to do it by spending less and producing more at home; the other leaned into fiscal expansion. The debate isn't about wanting affordability, it's about the tradeoffs.

Doc Riter's larger point is about means and ends. Tariffs aren't about prices in isolation - they're a means to challenge China's market dominance with the end goal of reasserting American leverage while integrating with trusted partners. But that strategic goal collides with domestic political reality: no democracy votes for steep tax hikes and spending cuts. Pet projects persist across parties, foreign policy swings, and checks and balances make hard tradeoffs nearly impossible. So debt keeps growing.

The real question isn't whether experts have good ideas. It's whether a technocratic approach can convince "needy humans" to accept the costs of those ideas. Without that political coalition, "unleashing the technocrats" is just another form of wishful thinking.

entries.title: 🎬 New York Times - Hollywood Thinks the Tech Oligarch Must Be Stopped
entries.content:
The New York Times suggests Hollywood has decided the tech oligarch must be stopped, framing Silicon Valley's power as the new existential threat worth dramatizing on screen. Doc Riter flips the lens: "Americans empowered by AI think Hollywood Must Be Stopped."

The core point is straightforward: technology itself isn't villainous just because a filmmaker made a movie about Zuckerberg. And tech founders aren't inherently liars, fabulists, or narcissists in any way that distinguishes them categorically from Hollywood.

That asymmetry is telling. Hollywood has spent decades mythmaking and shaping cultural narratives, often with little self-awareness about its own concentration of power and incentives. The industry that built its fortune on selling stories now frets about who controls the next storytelling machine.

Instead of a morality play pitting good creators against evil technologists, the more honest take is a competition over attention, distribution, and cultural influence. Both industries chase those things. Calling one side uniquely corrupt while the other rides to the rescue doesn't hold up. The power struggle is real, but the saints and villains are evenly distributed.

entries.title: ⛽ $10 Gas and Narrative Journalism
entries.content:
A recent New York Times front page story frames $10-per-gallon gas as a direct consequence of Trump being president, clearly positioning it as part of the "affordability crisis" angle ahead of the next election. Doc Riter takes a more skeptical read of what the story actually reports.

Buried in the details is a different reality: in that remote location, residents rent a gas generator for $5,000 a month because solar would cost $3 million to install. That single fact reframes the entire headline. The high cost isn't just "gas prices under Trump" so much as the structural economics of energy in a remote, isolated grid.

So the story is less about national inflation politics than about tradeoffs in extreme geography. But the framing leads readers to a predetermined conclusion: blame the president, blame the party in power. The nuance gets lost while the narrative fits neatly into a partisan message.

That's the distinction between reporting facts and crafting a narrative. When a story tells readers they're informed, but probing questions reveal context that undermines the headline, it's no longer straight news. It's advocacy packaged as reporting. And it erodes trust in the process more than any particular price ever could.

entries.title: 🕵️ Shilling and Sleuthing
entries.content:
The New York Times reports on the frenzied online hunt to identify Cornell's "Jane Doe" in a campus incident. Doc Riter's quip cuts both ways: what about the frenzied hunt by NYT trolls to identify Cornell's "Joe Suspect"?

The double standard is obvious. When amateur internet sleuths try to unmask a victim or piece together details, they're condemned as ghoulish, invasive, or reckless. But when major outlets engage in the same behavior - digging into identities, speculating, or feeding the very attention they're decrying - it gets a more respectable gloss.

The outrage depends on who's doing it. If it's anonymous posters on 4chan or X, it's a moral failing. If it's an investigative desk with a masthead, it's "public interest journalism." But the incentives and consequences look remarkably similar: clicks, attention, and the pressure to publish first.

Doc Riter's point isn't to defend online trolls. It's to point out the asymmetry. Journalistic ethics shouldn't bend depending on whether the keyboard belongs to a credentialed reporter or a random user. The principle - don't gratuitously expose private individuals or fuel mob identification - ought to apply across the board. Otherwise it's just shilling for one's own tribe.

entries.title: ✊ Mattering
entries.content:
The New York Times covers the latest round of "No Kings" rallies focusing on getting out the early vote. Doc Riter points to a photo-op moment: a white liberal woman in Prospect Park holding a sign that reads "because Black votes matter too."

The contradiction is stark. If the premise is that Black votes matter, the "too" implies they don't already - or that the movement needs to be reminded of it. It's a classic case of performative allyship where the focus subtly shifts back to the person holding the sign.

The sentiment might be well-intentioned, but the phrasing betrays a worldview that treats the cause as something the holder is graciously extending to others, rather than something rooted in basic equality. It centers the white ally rather than the people the message is supposedly about.

This is the kind of symbolic gesture that dominates modern protest culture: more concerned with signaling one's own virtue than with precision or clarity. The message doesn't persuade skeptics; it reassures the sign-holder that they matter for holding it. And that's the problem - when activism becomes primarily about self-affirmation, the actual goal gets lost.

No more colored bins. No more contamination fees. One collection stream, industrial-grade separation, measurable recovery rates. Municipalities save on collection logistics; facilities optimize throughput with AI-driven sort recipes that adapt to packaging changes in real time. The economics flip when sorting cost drops below landfill tipping fees — which it already has in pilots across EU and US.

entries.title: 💸 Big Tech doesn't want to hire American workers
entries.content:
'For every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one-and-a-half foreign indentured servants,' - Vice President Vance.
TechNet waited until the deadline to file its comment on the DHS proposal to charge $103,265 for every H-1B cap-subject petition, payable at filing and stacked on top of every other fee. The number is just $8,777,488,035 of interagency costs divided by 85,000 projected petitions, and the agency concedes assigning those costs to one slice of employers is a model it has never used before. The docket took 11,706 submissions in a 30-day window, which is a comment period sized for a footnote and not for an $8.8B annual charge.

TechNet's complaint is the one DHS put in its own record: the agency's analysis finds significant economic impact on 76% of the small businesses that filed cap-subject petitions in FY2025. Startups do not have five million employees to spread a six-figure charge across, so the work goes to an existing team in another country or the project slips. That is the interesting part of this rule, because the money is not really about who files an H-1B. It is about which employers can still afford to hire one.

The sharpest line is the advanced degree exemption. Congress reserved 20,000 cap slots for US graduates, and the proposal does not formally repeal them, it just charges the graduates $103,265 to use them. TechNet also wants no supplemental charge at all in the first cap cycle, capped at 5% of the proposal in the second and 10% in the third, payment deferred until after approval, refunds when a petition dies on a visa refusal, and an exemption for anyone holding a US master's or doctorate. Withdrawal remains the recommendation. The fallback schedule is a useful tell for what industry expects to actually happen: not withdrawal, but a fee that ratchets up over three years instead of one.

entries.title: 🎬 At Our Windows
entries.content:
I am at a window. I am on my phone. I can't stop watching videos of people reacting to the Minneapolis story. It's almost like a movie that doesn't end. So instead of augmenting that endless scroll, here is something LONG and something SHORT:

Sátántangó (1994) - Béla Tarr's 7+ hour masterpiece. Hypnotic, glacial, crushing. A film about waiting, dissolution, and the slow dissolution of hope. If you can survive it, you'll understand something about why we're compelled to watch endings we already know. Also available on Kanopy (free with library card).

"Monday" by Billy Collins

The birds are in their trees,
the toast is in the toaster,
and the poets are at their windows.

They are at their windows
in every section of the tangerine of earth—
the Chinese poets looking up at the moon,
the American poets gazing out
at the pink and blue ribbons of sunrise.

The clerks are at their desks,
the miners are down in their mines,
and the poets are looking out their windows
maybe with a cigarette, a cup of tea,
and maybe a flannel shirt or bathrobe is involved.

The proofreaders are playing the ping-pong
game of proofreading,
glancing back and forth from page to page,
the chefs are dicing celery and potatoes,
and the poets are at their windows
because it is their job for which
they are paid nothing every Friday afternoon.

Which window it hardly seems to matter
though many have a favorite,
for there is always something to see—
a bird grasping a thin branch,
the headlights of a taxi rounding a corner,
those two boys in wool caps angling across the street.

The fishermen bob in their boats,
the linemen climb their round poles,
the barbers wait by their mirrors and chairs,
and the poets continue to stare
at the cracked birdbath or a limb knocked down by the wind.

By now, it should go without saying
that what the oven is to the baker
and the berry-stained blouse to the dry cleaner,
so the window is to the poet.

Just think—
before the invention of the window,
the poets would have had to put on a jacket
and a winter hat to go outside
or remain indoors with only a wall to stare at.

And when I say a wall,
I do not mean a wall with striped wallpaper
and a sketch of a cow in a frame.

I mean a cold wall of fieldstones,
the wall of the medieval sonnet,
the original woman's heart of stone,
the stone caught in the throat of her poet-lover.


From The Trouble with Poetry and Other Poems. Read more

entries.title: ⚕️ MAID in America
entries.content:
"If a suffering New Yorker made the difficult choice to die, who am I to stand in their way?" - NY Governor Hochul.

I'm a suffering American and I hope there are people in power who would stand in my way. In melancholic moments I've contemplated or ideated on the end. I get it, mental illness doesn't count. But what does count, is that there are less and less people standing in my way. And there are less and less people standing for my way. Selfishness is pragmatic. Loss is ephemeral. The bad thoughts go away eventually. We prefer to be left alone, free to our own will, autonomous until the end when we lay flat together.

In crisis management we're taught to assess risk so that suicidal ideation is properly managed and walked down. The norm should always be to preserve innocent life; not to hasten death. Democrats smartly retort that it's not about shortening life but shortening death. But what the hell does that even mean? Life is pain. Life can be miserable. And we are all dying at a different pace. The slippery slope is to not speak truthfully about it. To dance around a hard truth is what a politician does. They are vapid; the results of an apathetic electorate. We should come to our senses before even feebly endorsing assisted suicide. We should face it directly and call it what it is. Medical aid in dying (MAID) is anesthetizing a harsh, blunt, and unpleasant end. It is the euphemism of the century. MAID may be practical and convenient. It is also an endorsement of taking innocent life. It also makes me feel empty inside. It makes me contemplate shortening my own death. I'm eventually inconvenient if not already. AI can do my job. But I reject a culture that placates despair. Do you?

Wandering elderly man in sneakers, jeans, and a sweatshirt.
A crew, 'for me to be happy in the city…'
Sitting still is not easy.
The world passes you by and it's completely indifferent.
The sun feels nice and the cable cars creak; comfort in cacophony and cacophony in comfort.
A weird word. A weird world.
